pitfall_name: WebGPU timestamp queries are optional, quantized, and absent in Safari
what_happens: GPU compute timing numbers are rounded to ~100µs granularity in Chrome, and Safari has no timestamp-query feature at all — so cross-browser GPU benchmarks either lie (Chrome) or cannot be measured (Safari).
why: The WebGPU spec makes timestamp-query an optional device feature; Chrome enables it by default but applies 100µs quantization for timing-attack mitigation. MDN compatibility tables show Safari (including Safari 26 / iOS 26) reports 'No support' for the timestamp value.
how_discovered: Benchmarks show suspiciously round numbers (multiples of 100µs) in Chrome, or adapter.features.has('timestamp-query') returns false in Safari — typically wastes hours trying to reconcile timing numbers across browsers.
mitigation: Feature-detect timestamp-query; if unavailable, fall back to CPU-side performance.now() bracketing (recognizing it includes submission/queue latency, not pure GPU time) and report it as 'wall-clock GPU submit-to-finish', never as 'GPU compute time'. Always disclose quantization in reported numbers.

what_happens: WASM pthreads / multi-worker proving pools construct SharedArrayBuffer and get a TypeError or undefined constructor; the entire multithreaded path dies at runtime in production while working fine on localhost.
why: Since Spectre (2018), browsers only expose SharedArrayBuffer in a cross-origin-isolated context. The page must send Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp (or credentialless). Without these, window.crossOriginIsolated is false and the constructor is unreachable.
how_discovered: Code that worked on localhost (where isolation is implicit) throws in production behind a CDN/proxy that strips or omits the headers. Often diagnosed only after a user reports a blank page or console TypeError.
mitigation: Set both COOP and COEP headers at the edge/server; verify with window.crossOriginIsolated. Audit all cross-origin subresources (analytics, fonts, ads, iframes) — COEP will block any that lack CORP or CORS. Provide a single-threaded fallback path when crossOriginIsolated is false.

what_happens: Large proving parameter sets (e.g. big Merkle trees, large FFT twiddles, large witness vectors) hit WebAssembly.Memory.grow() failures; allocation of a 256MiB scratch buffer hard-fails even when the system has free RAM.
why: WASM is currently an ILP32 process: pointers are 32-bit, hard-limiting linear memory to 4GiB. Some browsers enforce even lower effective ceilings. The memory64 (wasm64) proposal is still not widely available in browser engines.
how_discovered: Allocation throws RuntimeError: memory access out of bounds or grow_memory returns -1 mid-proof. Typically found when scaling to larger circuit sizes; smaller test circuits work fine.
mitigation: Chunk the workload: stream witness/proof data in segments that fit under ~3GiB; use SharedArrayBuffer for inter-worker data instead of duplicating in each worker's own linear memory; consider WebGPU storage buffers for large read-only tables; prefer 64-bit if the target runtime supports memory64 behind a flag.

pitfall_name: JS↔WASM data marshalling dominates proving time
what_happens: Profile shows the majority of wall-clock time is spent copying field elements / witness data between JS TypedArrays and WASM linear memory, not in the actual finite-field arithmetic.
why: WASM cannot directly read JS heap objects. Every call that passes arrays requires either copying into linear memory (via HEAPU8.set()) or meticulous pointer management. Naive implementations that round-trip data per kernel invocation multiply this cost.
how_discovered: Benchmark shows throughput far below native expectations; profiling reveals memcpy-equivalent operations dominating the profile. Usually wastes days of optimization effort before the marshalling overhead is recognized.
mitigation: Allocate once in linear memory and operate in-place; pass offsets/pointers instead of array contents; use compileStreaming + instance caching; batch many small calls into one large call to amortize the boundary crossing; consider using WASM Component Model or Embind's direct memory access patterns.

pitfall_name: WebGPU readback stalls masquerade as compute time
what_happens: Reported 'GPU proving time' includes mapAsync() wait time where the CPU blocks until the GPU finishes and the buffer is transferred — this can be 2-10× the actual compute duration, and overlaps with subsequent JS work in non-obvious ways.
why: GPUBuffer.mapAsync(GPUMapMode.READ) returns a promise that resolves only after the GPU has completed all prior submitted work AND the buffer is mapped for CPU access. If you await it immediately after queue.submit(), you serialize CPU and GPU unnecessarily.
how_discovered: Benchmark numbers are wildly inconsistent run-to-run; CPU utilization shows the main thread blocked. Diagnosed when someone adds a second compute pass and notices it doesn't overlap with the first as expected.
mitigation: Double-buffer: submit N work items, then read back result N-2 while N-1 and N are still on GPU; use onSubmittedWorkDone() only when you truly need strict ordering; measure GPU time via timestamp queries (see pitfall #1) separately from readback latency; never count mapAsync await time as compute.

pitfall_name: JIT warmup and tiering distort WASM benchmarks
what_happens: First proof in a session runs 3-10× slower than subsequent proofs; naive benchmarking reports the cold-run number as 'performance', underestimating real throughput by a wide margin.
why: V8 (and other engines) initially compiles WASM with a fast-but-slow Liftoff compiler, then recompiles hot functions with the optimizing TurboFan backend. The tiering happens during the first executions. Additionally, the WASM module itself has parse/instantiate cost on first load.
how_discovered: Running the same proof twice yields drastically different timings; benchmark suites that don't discard warmup iterations report misleading numbers. Typically wastes significant time chasing a 'performance regression' that is just cold-start.
mitigation: Always discard ≥3 warmup iterations before timing; report median/percentile over many runs; use WebAssembly.compileStreaming to overlap download and compilation; consider that on mobile, tiering thresholds may differ from desktop.

pitfall_name: GC pauses attributed to proving workload
what_happens: Mid-proof timing spikes of 50-200ms appear irregularly; benchmarking attributes them to 'the cryptography' when they are actually V8 garbage collection pauses from JS-side allocations in the driver code.
why: If the JS orchestration layer allocates temporary arrays, objects, or closures per proof step (common in naive witness generation or proof assembly), V8's young-generation GC will pause the main thread. These pauses are non-deterministic and depend on heap pressure.
how_discovered: Box plots of proof time show occasional outliers 5-20× the median. Tracing with V8 GC flags (--trace-gc) reveals the correlation. Usually misdiagnosed as 'GPU stalls' or 'network latency' first.
mitigation: Pre-allocate all JS-side buffers and reuse them across proofs; avoid per-step closures and array literals; use ArrayBuffer/TypedArray pools; measure with GC paused (e.g., --gc-interval large) for microbenchmarks, but report real-world numbers with GC enabled and disclose variance.

pitfall_name: SIMD not actually vectorizing field arithmetic
what_happens: Field multiplication compiled with simd128 enabled shows little to no speedup over scalar code, despite expectations of 2-4× throughput improvement.
why: WASM SIMD operates on 128-bit vectors of integers, but cryptographic fields (e.g., 256-bit BN254, 381-bit BLS12-381) don't map neatly to 128-bit lanes. The compiler may emit scalar fallbacks for 256-bit+ operations, or the algorithm (Montgomery / CIOS) may not have a natural 4-wide decomposition. Relaxed SIMD can help but trades cross-platform bit-exactness.
how_discovered: Enabling -msimd128 in Emscripten produces a binary that runs at the same speed; inspection of generated WASM shows scalar opcodes, not v128 operations. Wastes time assuming 'SIMD is on, so it must be faster'.
mitigation: Explicitly hand-vectorize the innermost prime-field multiply using 64-bit lane operations where the field modulus allows (e.g., 255-bit curves can pack into 4×64-bit lanes); verify vectorization by disassembling the WASM or checking for v128 opcodes; benchmark before/after, not assumption.

pitfall_name: Mobile browser memory kills during large proofs
what_happens: The browser tab crashes or the OS kills the page mid-proof on mobile, with no JS exception — particularly during grow_memory or large TypedArray allocations.
why: Mobile browsers enforce aggressive memory limits (often 2-4GB total per tab depending on device) and the OS may kill the renderer under memory pressure. Additionally, some mobile browsers cap WASM linear memory below the 4GiB theoretical maximum.
how_discovered: Proofs that work on desktop crash on iPhone/Samsung with no error message; the tab simply reloads or closes. Diagnosed via mobile DevTools remote debugging showing 'Renderer process exited' or OOM kills.
mitigation: Proactively limit working set to <1GB on mobile; stream witness data in chunks; detect navigator.deviceMemory and degrade gracefully (smaller proof batch, fewer worker threads); add beforeunload checkpointing so a killed proof can resume; avoid allocating large contiguous buffers upfront.

pitfall_name: iframe / embedded context SharedArrayBuffer and WebGPU denial
what_happens: A proving widget embedded via <iframe> from a different origin silently loses SAB (and thus pthreads) and/or WebGPU, even though the parent page is properly isolated.
why: Cross-origin iframes inherit isolation only when the embedding document grants the cross-origin-isolated permission via Permissions-Policy. Similarly, WebGPU in a cross-origin iframe requires the iframe's own origin to serve the proper headers AND the parent to delegate the permission. Nested documents and workers each need COEP set.
how_discovered: Embedded widget works standalone but fails inside the host page's iframe; crossOriginIsolated is false in the iframe context. Often discovered late in integration testing.
mitigation: Both parent and iframe must send COOP/COEP; the parent must include Permissions-Policy: cross-origin-isolated 'self' https://widget-origin. For WebGPU, ensure the iframe's origin also serves the headers. Test in the actual embedded context, not just standalone.

pitfall_name: Safari WebGPU divergence in supported features
what_happens: A compute pipeline that runs perfectly on Chrome fails on Safari with validation errors or silent incorrect results, despite both 'supporting WebGPU'.
why: Safari 26.0+ ships WebGPU by default (macOS Tahoe 26, iOS 26, iPadOS 26, visionOS 26), but feature coverage differs: timestamp queries are unsupported, and some features may be flagged experimental or behave differently. Firefox support is still partial (Windows in 141+, macOS Apple Silicon in 147+, Linux/Android in progress).
how_discovered: Cross-browser test reveals Safari throwing GPUValidationError on a pipeline that Chrome accepts. Diagnosed by comparing adapter.features sets and reading WebKit bug tracker reports.
mitigation: Feature-detect every optional WebGPU feature before use (adapter.features.has(...)); provide graceful degradation for missing features; test on actual Safari (not just Chrome) early in development; avoid experimental Dawn-specific toggles in production code.

pitfall_name: WASM threads worker pool and Atomics.wait blocking
what_happens: A pool of WASM pthreads appears to 'hang' or make no progress; CPU shows threads sleeping but no work being done.
why: Emscripten's pthreads use Atomics.wait() for blocking synchronization on SharedArrayBuffer. If the main thread or another worker fails to call Atomics.notify(), the waiting threads sleep indefinitely. Additionally, if crossOriginIsolated is false, pthreads spawn falls back to a single-threaded emulation that may silently serialize all work.
how_discovered: Profiler shows worker threads in Atomics.wait syscall; no progress after main thread posts work. Often diagnosed after hours of wondering why 'multithreaded' code is actually slower than single-threaded.
mitigation: Verify crossOriginIsolated before spawning workers; ensure every Atomics.wait() has a corresponding Atomics.notify(); use Atomics.notify(loc, idx, count) with correct count; consider a work-stealing scheduler instead of blocking waits; add timeouts/logging to detect deadlocks during development.
